course.learn: A brute-force attack systematically tries many possible credentials, keys, or values until one works. It trades time and computing power for certainty.
course.why: Weak or short secrets make exhaustive guessing practical.
course.example: An attacker tries every four-digit PIN from 0000 through 9999.
course.exam: Brute force = exhaustive guessing. Password spraying uses a small number of common passwords across many accounts; dictionary attacks use likely words/passwords.

course.learn: Backups create recoverable copies of data or systems so organizations can restore after deletion, corruption, ransomware, or disaster. Good backup strategy considers location, frequency, retention, immutability, encryption, and restore testing.
course.why: A backup is valuable only if it survives the incident and can actually be restored within business requirements.
course.example: An organization keeps frequent local backups for speed plus protected offsite/immutable copies so ransomware cannot destroy every recovery point.
course.exam: Know onsite vs offsite, snapshots vs true backups, restore testing, and the fact that replication does not replace historical backup copies.

course.learn: Environmental attacks or incidents affect the physical conditions supporting technology—power, temperature, water, fire, ventilation, and facility controls. Tampering with environmental systems can become a security incident.
course.why: Hardware can fail or become unavailable even when software and network controls are functioning correctly.
course.example: An attacker disables cooling in a server room, causing temperature alarms and equipment shutdowns.
course.exam: Look for changes in temperature/power, damaged environmental controls, alarms, or physical tampering.

breakdown.explanation: Hardware security risk includes vulnerable firmware, malicious peripherals, insecure interfaces, unsupported devices, and physical tampering.
